content.title: Apollo 13 Set The Record Artemis II Just Broke, But That Wasn’t The Plan
content.text: Artemis II's flight path (not to scale) as imagined by an artist for NASANASAThe Artemis II astronauts are now farther from Earth than any humans have ever gone.A little before 2:00 Eastern Daylight Time on Monday afternoon, the crew’s Orion capsule whizzed past the 400,171-kilometer mark, officially breaking the record Apollo 13 set in 1970. A few hours later, on the far side of the Moon and out of radio contact with Earth, Artemis II set its own record: 406,778 miles from Earth and nearly every other human being in the universe (not counting the crew of the International Space Station, who will be a few hundred kilometers closer to Artemis II than the rest of us).Apollo 13's closest approach to the Moon was about 254 kilometers, and at the far end of its figure-eight path, it was 400,171 kilometers from Earth – a record that lasted for more than 50 years, until Artemis II. But Apollo 13 was never supposed to set a record. Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert, and Fred Haise (who, fun fact, were all “Junior,” named for evidently uncreative fathers) were just trying to get home, and their only way back to Earth was the long way around the Moon – farther than anyone had ever gone before.Flying Figure-Eights Around The MoonArtemis II is, essentially, flying in a giant figure-eight pattern around the Moon and back. Rocket scientists call this a free-return trajectory (or a circumlunar trajectory, but “free-return” sounds cooler), and it saves fuel by using the Moon’s gravity like a slingshot to help send the Orion capsule coasting back home again. (Mission planners often use moons’ and planets’ gravity to help spacecraft speed up or slow down; these “gravity assists” help missions like Voyager 1 and 2 and New Horizons reach the outer Solar System without needing wildly impractical amounts of fuel.)For missions that want to orbit or land anywhere near the Moon’s equator, the free-return trajectory is the shortest route. (Artemis I took a longer but more fuel-efficient route, which is the kind of tradeoff that mission planners can make with uncrewed flights but not with astronauts on board.) The first crewed flights to visit lunar orbit – Apollos 8, 10, and 11 – flew on free-return trajectories, as did the first (uncrewed) lunar orbiter, Luna 3.Mission planners can vary the size and proportions of their free-return figure-eight depending on how close they want to get to the Moon, when they want to enter lunar orbit, and so on. Artemis II is flying on a much wider, longer loop than any of the Apollo missions, for example – which is why it just broke Apollo 13’s record.But Apollo 13 was never supposed to set a record in the first place. Its crew just wanted to get home.The Long Way HomeApollo 13 was more than halfway to the Moon, about 330,000 kilometers from Earth, when one of the ship’s oxygen tanks exploded. The explosion – caused, as it later turned out, by a spark from a wire with damaged insulation – knocked out the electrical and life support systems in the command and service module, the main part of the ship where the astronauts were meant to live on the way to the Moon and back. Lovell, Swigert, and Haise had to seek shelter in the lunar module, which meant stuffing three men into a space designed for two – and making its resources and systems stretch for three days instead of the planned two. With limited power, temperatures in the capsule hovered just above freezing; water condensed on the walls, but the crew had little to drink – every possible drop had to be saved for cooling the spacecraft’s equipment. Swigert suffered through the whole thing with wet feet.If the beleaguered ship and crew stayed on their original course, they would loop around the Moon but miss Earth on the way back. And they couldn’t just turn around and drive home; that’s just not how spaceflight works. At that point in the flight, Apollo 13 was under the Moon’s gravitational influence, not Earth’s, and it would have taken too much power (and therefore too much fuel) to break free of the Moon’s grip and power back toward Earth.Changing course in space is really a matter of changing speed (engineers and astronauts call this delta-V, from the “delta” symbol for change and “V” for velocity). Haise used the lunar module’s descent propulsion system – the thrusters that were supposed to be for landing on the Moon and taking off again – to change Apollo 13’s velocity just enough to put it on a free-return trajectory, in which the Moon’s gravity would help sling the spacecraft toward home.The first step in getting home would be riding the free-return trajectory past the Moon. The previous Apollo missions had orbited the Moon at an altitude of about 110 kilometers, which meant that when the command module passed “behind” the far side of the Moon, it was only about 110 kilometers beyond the Moon itself. Apollo 13, though, would sweep 252 kilometers past the Moon before swinging back toward home – farther than anyone had ever flown, all while the rocky bulk of the Moon blocked Earth from sight and cut off communication, leaving the three men huddled in the cold, damp lunar module alone in the vast black.And they had to do it in a damaged spacecraft with dwindling power.The Artemis II crew has it easy by comparison – then again, they’re flying thousands of kilometers farther, and they’re doing it in a spacecraft no one has ever actually flown in before, which has already had multiple issues with its toilets. When you’re flying to the Moon, there’s no such thing as easy. It’s an adventure, and adventures are, in the words of one Bilbo Baggins, “Nasty disturbing uncomfortable things [that] make you late for dinner!”
